sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: System design rounds are now standard at mid-to-senior Go engineer interviews. Interviewers want to see that you can reason about trade-offs—throughput vs. latency, consistency vs. availability—and map those decisions onto concrete Go services. Go's lightweight goroutines and small binary footprint make certain architectural choices (stateless edge services, high-concurrency API gateways) a natural fit, and knowing why makes your answers stand out.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: Think of any system design problem in four layers: (1) Estimate — QPS, data volume, bandwidth. (2) Partition — where does the data live and how is it split? (3) Route — load balancing, consistent hashing, caching. (4) Protect — rate limiting, circuit breakers, back-pressure. Go services typically sit at layers 3 and 4 as high-throughput request handlers; understanding layers 1–2 lets you justify your concurrency and connection-pool settings with numbers.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body: 1. Capacity estimation: back-of-envelope math (QPS = DAU × requests/day ÷ 86 400). 2. Caching: cache-aside vs. write-through vs. write-behind; TTL, eviction (LRU), thundering herd. 3. Load balancing: round-robin, least-connections, consistent hashing for session stickiness. 4. CAP theorem: CP (Zookeeper, HBase) vs. AP (Cassandra, DynamoDB) and when to choose each. 5. Consistent hashing: virtual nodes, why it minimises key remapping when nodes join/leave. 6. Rate limiting: token bucket vs. leaky bucket vs. sliding-window log; Go implementation with time.Ticker or golang.org/x/time/rate. 7. Database sharding: range vs. hash sharding, hot-shard problem, cross-shard queries.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body: • 'Walk me through how you would design a URL shortener end-to-end.' → leads to capacity estimation + consistent hashing + caching. • 'How would you rate-limit an API that serves 50 k RPS?' → token bucket, Redis + Lua script, or in-process golang.org/x/time/rate with a sync.Map per key. • 'How do you decide between SQL and NoSQL?' → CAP theorem, access patterns, eventual consistency tolerance. • 'What happens when one cache node goes down?' → consistent hashing minimises redistribution; hot-spot mitigation with local L1 cache in Go process.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "Before jumping into components, I always start with a quick capacity estimate. For this problem I'd assume X DAU, Y requests per user per day, which gives roughly Z QPS at peak. That tells me I need at least N stateless Go service instances behind a load balancer. I'd use consistent hashing to distribute cache keys across Redis nodes so that adding a node only remaps 1/N of keys. For rate limiting I'd reach for golang.org/x/time/rate in-process for per-goroutine limits, backed by a Redis sliding-window for distributed enforcement. The CAP trade-off here favours AP because users can tolerate seeing slightly stale data, so I'd pick DynamoDB for the primary store."
